name: Esther Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own a small electric van, paid for in cash, and I work three apps at once. Mornings I grab a four-hour parcel block from the depot at Westgate business park, then grocery deliveries in the afternoon, and takeaway if the evening surge looks good. I've only been at it six months and I'm still slower than most at the scanning and the building numbers. What I love is that I'm my own boss of the day; what I don't love is my lower back after sixty parcels.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you decide which app to work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a chatbot on my phone that I talk to every morning. I paste in yesterday's earnings and the weather and ask it which blocks pay best per hour, and it's usually right. I used to work in a call centre, and I left three years ago because I could see the software taking over the scripts. I saved most of what I earned there, so I've got the van and about a year's money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, now let's talk about the actual problem, which is that three companies set the pay for thousands of drivers. I'd post about a drivers' co-op app, where we own the platform. People would say I'm dreaming, and I'd say so were the people who started the first unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep doing what I'm doing and get better at it. I'd like to be faster at the depot and work fewer hours for the same money. Nothing in this picture threatens me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my three-app system and my chatbot planning every morning. I'd spend the winter learning the depot routes properly so I'm not wasting twenty minutes per block. I'd also join the drivers' co-op meetings in town and help them build a sign-up form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe, because I like when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You left a call centre because of software. Would you feel you'd moved too soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd have left anyway; I hated reading scripts to angry people. The van is mine and I choose my hours. Even if AI stalls, I'm happier out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still bothers you about the job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, and the fact that the apps can change the rules. The parcel app cut the rate for blocks in the rain last month, which is exactly when it's hardest. My van is paid for and I've got a year in the bank, so a bad month is annoying, not scary.

say: I'd say the real problem is **three companies** setting pay for thousands of drivers.
I'd post about a **drivers' co-op app** that the drivers own themselves.
think: Nothing here **threatens me** much; I keep improving at the job.
I'd like to get **faster at the depot** and earn the same in fewer hours.
do: Keep the **three-app system** with the chatbot planning each morning.
Learn the **depot routes** properly over the winter to save twenty minutes a block.
Help the **drivers' co-op** build its sign-up form.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored, because she likes when things move.
S0.quote: My van is paid for and I've got a year in the bank, so a bad month is annoying, not scary.
fieldNote: She already **left a job** once because she saw software coming.
Uses a **chatbot daily** to choose which app to work, unusual for a junior driver.
Her **owned van** and a year of savings make her secure.
Progressive hope rests on a **drivers' co-op**, not just regulation.

steps.text: Keep working three apps from the paid-off electric van
Ask the chatbot each morning which delivery blocks pay best
Build the sign-up form for the town's drivers' co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, to my old call centre friends. Online I'd push for rules that make the apps share their data with drivers. And I'd say this is when a co-op app actually becomes possible, because the software to run one gets cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for me. My driving and lifting stays mine for years, and the planning gets easier. If the apps get smarter, I'll use smarter tools too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try every new tool that helps drivers pick routes and stack orders. I'd try to get the co-op to build a basic app using AI coding tools, and I'd help test it with my van. I'd keep about a year's money untouched no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like a new season starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking tasks go first. What does that mean for the app side of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the dispatch and support stuff, the people who used to answer driver emails, gets replaced. But somebody still has to physically put a bag of shopping on a doorstep, and that's why I like being on this side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go back to an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a call centre, never. Maybe an office that runs delivery robots one day. I'd want to be the person who knows how both the van and the software work.

say: I'd push for rules making apps **share their data** with drivers.
I'd say cheap software finally makes a **co-op app** possible.
think: This is **mostly good** for me, because my lifting stays mine for years.
If the apps get **smarter**, I'll use smarter tools too.
do: Try every **new tool** that helps drivers stack orders and pick routes.
Help the co-op build a **basic app** with AI coding tools and test it.
Keep **a year's money** untouched whatever happens.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like a new season starting.
S1.quote: Somebody still has to physically put a bag of shopping on a doorstep, and that's why I like being on this side of it.
fieldNote: She reads the scenario precisely: **dispatch and support** go, the doorstep stays.
Sees **opportunity**, including a driver-owned app.
Her past **call centre** exit gives her confidence she reads change well.
Wants to know both **the van** and **the software**.

steps.text: Test new route-stacking tools on the parcel and grocery apps
Help build and test a drivers' co-op app made with AI coding
Keep a full year of living costs untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for drivers today, not in 2031, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd push the co-op to ask the council for retraining money. I'd be honest that delivery as we know it is ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I have about four good years left in the van. I'm young and I've got money, so I'm not terrified, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried. Even the job I fancy, running robots, could be done by AGI by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a course in electric vehicle and robot maintenance this year, while still driving. I'd sell the van in 2029 or 2030, before every driver tries to sell theirs at once. I'd also use AI every day to learn the technical side faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Scared and excited at the same time, like the first morning I took the van out on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots can deliver by 2031, what's your plan for the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell it early, before the market fills with used delivery vans. I'd rather lose a bit by selling the van early than be stuck with a van nobody wants. Then the money goes into training and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. Is there a version where it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the robots come early and the maintenance jobs go to people with degrees. Then I'm twenty-nine with a nice CV for a job that's gone. That's why I'd keep a year of money no matter what.

say: I'd say drivers need a **plan today**, not in 2031.
I'd be honest that **delivery** as we know it is ending.
think: I have about **four good years** left in the van.
Even the job I want, **running robots**, could be done by AGI by then.
do: Start a course in **robot maintenance** this year while still driving.
**Sell the van** in 2029 or 2030, before every driver does.
Keep **a year's money** in reserve no matter what.
feel: **Wired**: scared and excited at the same time.
S2.quote: I'd rather lose a bit by selling the van early than be stuck with a van nobody wants.
fieldNote: Even this adaptive driver expects her **income to change** within five years.
Plans to **sell the van early**, thinking ahead of the crowd.
Admits a real risk: maintenance jobs might **need degrees**.
Money gives her **control**, so anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Enrol in an electric vehicle and robot maintenance course this year
Sell the electric van in 2029 before the used market floods
Keep a year of living costs in savings throughout
Use a chatbot daily to study the technical course material

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we should use it, and the co-op should plan for drivers to own some of the robots. I'd post that a lot. Drivers owning the robots is the only version where we're not just thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a good amount of time for me. I could drive for four or five more years and train on the side. I'd be thirty-four when the robots get good, with skills and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving full time for two years and put more into savings. Then I'd start the maintenance course and maybe try a remote robot supervisor job. I'd also want the co-op to buy two or three delivery robots as a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but in a good way. Like before an exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra years buy you compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to try things and fail. With two years I'd have to pick one route and pray, but with five I can test a course, test a job and change my mind once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Priya, who works at a call centre like I used to. I'd drag her to the course with me. And the drivers in the co-op who don't speak much English.

say: I'd say drivers should **own** some of the **robots** through the co-op.
We have **a window**, and we should use it.
think: Five years is a **good amount** of time for me.
I'd be **thirty-four** with skills and money when robots get good.
do: Drive full time for **two years** and save more.
Start the **maintenance course** and try a remote robot supervisor job.
Push the co-op to **buy two or three** delivery robots as a test.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like before an exam she's studied for.
S3.quote: With two years I'd have to pick one route and pray, but with five I can test a course, test a job and change my mind once.
fieldNote: The extra time gives her **room to fail**, which she values.
Her co-op idea grows into **drivers owning robots**.
Thinks of others, like her flatmate **Priya** in a call centre.
Still sees her **driving ending**, so not fully calm.

steps.text: Drive full time for two more years and save more
Start the robot maintenance course in the third year
Put savings into the co-op's test of three delivery robots
Bring flatmate Priya and other drivers to co-op meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version, if we use it. I'd keep pushing the co-op and rules for fair pay. I'd tell people ten years is long enough to plan, not long enough to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's great. I'll be thirty-nine when the robots come, and I'd have had a full career of change by then. I'd probably not be driving at all by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my three-app system for a few years, then shift into planning or fixing. I'd save a big chunk and invest some in a fund. I'd keep using AI tools daily so I'm always ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit hopeful, which isn't how I expected to feel about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots around 2039. Does the long timeline change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think in ten years I could run a small fleet for the co-op. Drivers would be the owners and the robots would do the stairs. That's the dream version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chats at the depot, and the old man on Elm Close who always has the kettle on. Robots won't get the cup of tea.

say: Ten years is **long enough to plan**, not long enough to ignore.
I'd keep pushing the co-op and **fair pay rules**.
think: This is **great for me**; I'd likely stop driving by 2032.
I'd have a **whole career** of change behind me by thirty-nine.
do: Keep the **three-app system** for a few years, then move into planning or fixing.
Save a big chunk and **invest** some in a fund.
Use **AI tools** daily to stay ahead.
S4.quote: Drivers would be the owners and the robots would do the stairs. That's the dream version.
fieldNote: The long timeline makes her **hopeful** about a driver-owned fleet.
Plans to **leave driving** well before robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep the three-app delivery routine for a few more years
Invest part of the savings in a broad share fund
Use AI tools daily to learn fleet planning
Move into running the co-op's robot fleet by the early 2030s

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I can't learn fast enough for that, and the jobs I'm aiming for might vanish too. What would help is cheap, quick technical training while you still work, and some way for drivers to own part of the robots that replace us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask us what we'd build. People always ask what we're scared of. A lot of drivers have ideas about how this should work.

headlineQuote: Drivers owning the robots is the only version where we're not just thrown out.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** driver with a paid-off electric van who works three apps at once.
She left a **call centre** years ago because she saw software coming.
She uses a **chatbot daily** and has about a year of savings.
Her progressive answer is a **drivers' co-op** that could one day own robots.
She's **calm** in slower pictures and anxious only when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the technical jobs she's aiming for could vanish too.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, quick technical training** while still working.
A way for drivers to **own part** of the robots that replace them.
